title: Perioperative evaluation of endothelial function with the Acumen IQ Cuff by Edwards: Proof of concept
summary:
Maintaining a sufficient oxygen supply to the tissue during the operation through the blood circulation is an essential aspect of anaesthesia management. Until now, this control has been based exclusively on blood pressure, which is measured either by means of a blood pressure cuff ("non-invasive") or in an artery ("invasive"). However, the results of studies in recent years show that this information is only part of the puzzle. There are disturbances in the control of vessel width, which is essential for the control of blood supply in the tissue, independent of blood pressure. The innermost layer of blood vessels ("the endothelium") plays an important role in controlling blood supply in the smallest vessels ("the microcirculation") and normally influences vasodilatation through the release of vasodilating or vasoconstricting substances. This release is mainly triggered by local stimuli that adjust the vasodilatation to the blood flow and oxygen requirements of the tissue. This adaptation process can be disturbed ("endothelial dysfunction"). We are currently unable to measure this dysfunction as part of routine clinical practice.
However, there are methods for assessing this endothelial function that are used in scientific studies. In particular, "peripheral arterial tonometry" should be mentioned here, in which the change in vessel width is measured following an oxygen deficiency in the tissue. This involves inflating a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm for 5 minutes so that the blood supply in the arm is cut off, thereby triggering hypoxia. The pressure is then released from the cuff and the blood vessels should dilate due to the resulting oxygen deficiency. This dilation can be measured using a finger clip, which records the change in blood vessel width. Such a finger clip has been available for several years for measuring blood pressure and other circulatory parameters via the change in blood vessel width during an operation. We want to investigate whether the measurement described here can be carried out with it.

interventions.name:
Group 1 (n=40)
Age 18-35 years
Surgical intervention with low risk
No risk factors for endothelial dysfunction

Group 2 (n=10)
Age >=45 years
Surgical procedure with high risk and duration >2 hours
At least 2 risk factors for endothelial dysfunction

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Group 1 (n=40)
Age 18-35 years
Surgical intervention with low risk
No risk factors for endothelial dysfunction
- Group 2 (n=10)
Age >=45 years
Surgical procedure with high risk and duration >2 hours
At least 2 risk factors for endothelial dysfunction
Exclusion criteria:
Age <18 years.
 Pregnancy and breastfeeding
 Septic patients
 Patients with calcium antagonists or nitrate medication
 Patients with long-term corticosteroid therapy
 Emergency interventions
 Patients with Raynaud's syndrome and/or peripheral arterial disease and/or vasculitis
 Patients undergoing surgical procedures with tourniquets
